newsitem.title: USA: As 'quit rate' rises, so do US wage pressure fears.
newsitem.headline: As 'quit rate' rises, so do US wage pressure fears.

text.p: "I quit!"
For the better part of the 1990s those two words have been slow coming from employees' mouths as fears of finding a new job at an equal or better salary kept people from leaving.
But recent data show the number of those voluntarily leaving their jobs is on the rise, which some analysts believe is yet another sign of a U.S. labor market tight enough to elicit wage pressures.

"If you are willing to quit to become unemployed, you must feel quite confident about the labor market and the chances of finding a new job at better pay," said John Williams, chief global economist at Bankers Trust Co.

There are a number of ways of gauging voluntary job leavers, which economists call the "quit rate." The most widely cited indicator is the percentage rate of job leavers of total unemployed, which rose to 12.3 percent in January from 11.7 percent in December. In January 1995, for example, the rate was 9.3 percent.
The rate has been on the rise for three straight months, after keeping near the 11 percent range for much of 1996.

"When the quit rate jumps up like this, labor cost pressures are just around the corner," Williams said. "Since it has been largely steady until recently suggests one reason why inflation pressures haven't emerged yet."

The decline in the quit rate comes as the percentage of those fired from jobs dropped (to 44.8 percent in January). Re-entrants (34.6 percent) to the job market were also down, while first time job seekers (7.7 percent) rose a bit.

The issue of voluntary job leavers came to the forefront last week when Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan noted there is less job-hopping currently than one would normally expect at this late stage in the business cycle.

As such, economists said the rate would be one of the key indicators -- along with non-farm payrolls, average hourly earnings and the civilian jobless rate -- they will look at closely on Friday morning, when the Labor Department releases the February employment report.

"We haven't really seen anything yet, but if the increases persist another month or two, it would look as if the trend has changed," said Louis Crandall, chief economist at R.H. Wrightson & Associates.

"What is interesting is that (the quit rate) and wages have deviated from the normal pattern," with the quit rate rising, while wages remain mostly steady, he said. "If one starts coming back into line, perhaps the other is as well."
Crandall and others stressed the quit rate is just one measure of potential wage pressures and must be looked at along with other data.
But critics said the 12.3 percent quit rate is not that high, especially compared with the 14 percent level seen in the late 1970s and 16 percent in the mid to late 1980s.

Furthermore, some pointed to a separate measure of voluntary job leavers showing less of a threat to wage pressures, since the percentage of so-called quitters as a percentage of the total U.S. workforce rose 0.1 percent in January. Of the 5.4 percent jobless rate, just 0.7 percent came from voluntary job leavers, up a notch from 0.6 percent in December.

Still, the fact that the rate rose signals possible wage increases down the road, analysts said. "When you see the quit rate up, you are more than likely to believe you are closer to wage acceleration," said Marc Wanshel, an economist at J.P. Morgan & Co Inc. "But it is just one indicator of labor tightness."
If the quit rate rises along with jobless claims and high levels of consumer confidence on the job market front, "you could presume that the combination would lead to wage pressures," Wanshel said.
That being the case, and with Greenspan hinting at a pre-emptive strike on inflation, the Fed should raise rates as soon as possible, Bankers Trust's Williams said.

Once wages start to go up, "it's hard to turn around," Williams said. "Given the glacial speed at which the inflation process moves, it would really be preferred to move pre-emptively before the process gets started."
